title: Production Backend Thinking

topics.title: Observability
topics.description: Observability provides evidence for explaining system behavior from its outputs.
learningGoals: Signals support named operational questions
Credential values are excluded
examples: Refresh failures rise while latency increases.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Observability provides evidence for explaining system behavior from its outputs. Combine structured events, numerical trends, and request traces with meaningful identifiers. Decide which questions you need to answer before emitting large volumes of telemetry.

workedExample.scenario: Refresh failures rise while latency increases.
steps: Use metrics to locate the trend.
Use safe logs and traces to investigate affected operations.

commonMistakes: More logs are not automatically better observability.
guidedExercise: Choose three questions about refresh behavior
material.independentExercise: Design telemetry for successful, rejected, and failed rotation without raw tokens.
recallQuestions: What question does this signal answer?
How do you distinguish rejection from outage?

acceptanceCriteria: Signals support named operational questions
Credential values are excluded

topics.title: Logging
topics.description: Logs record discrete events with context useful for diagnosis.
learningGoals: Logs contain useful safe context
Success and failure paths redact credentials
examples: A refresh attempt is rejected for reuse.

tasks.title: Explain Logging in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Logs record discrete events with context useful for diagnosis. Prefer stable fields, safe identifiers, and explicit outcomes. Never log passwords, raw tokens, or unrestricted request bodies; useful diagnostics must respect secret boundaries.

workedExample.scenario: A refresh attempt is rejected for reuse.
steps: Log session ID, reason, and correlation ID.
Omit the presented token and Authorization header.

commonMistakes: Debug logging can still leak credentials even if normal logs are safe.
material.independentExercise: Audit success and failure logs for accidental secret inclusion.
recallQuestions: Which identifier can safely correlate events?
What must never be logged?

acceptanceCriteria: Logs contain useful safe context
Success and failure paths redact credentials

topics.title: Metrics
learningGoals: Metric dimensions have bounded values
Latency and failure categories support investigation
examples: Record refresh outcomes by a small reason set.

tasks.title: Explain Metrics in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Metrics summarize behavior over time. Track traffic, error rates, latency, and saturation with bounded label sets. High-cardinality labels such as arbitrary user or token IDs can make metric storage expensive and difficult to query.

workedExample.scenario: Record refresh outcomes by a small reason set.
steps: Count success and rejection.
Track duration without a per-user label.

commonMistakes: Every identifier is not a suitable metric dimension.
material.independentExercise: Define one useful alert and explain what investigation follows it.
recallQuestions: Why can user-ID labels be costly?
What does an average latency hide?

acceptanceCriteria: Metric dimensions have bounded values
Latency and failure categories support investigation

topics.title: Retries
topics.description: Retry only when failure may be transient and repeating the action is safe under its contract.
learningGoals: Retries cannot create extra effects
Attempt and time budgets are explicit
examples: A dependency times out after possibly accepting a request.

tasks.title: Explain Retries in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Retry only when failure may be transient and repeating the action is safe under its contract. Use a total deadline, bounded attempts, and backoff. Multiple retrying layers can multiply load and make an outage worse.

workedExample.scenario: A dependency times out after possibly accepting a request.
steps: Consult the idempotency contract.
Retry within a bounded budget or reconcile the uncertain outcome.

commonMistakes: Timeout does not prove the action was never performed.
material.independentExercise: Design a bounded notification retry without duplicate business effects.
recallQuestions: Which failures justify retry?
What happens when every layer retries?

acceptanceCriteria: Retries cannot create extra effects
Attempt and time budgets are explicit

topics.title: Idempotency
topics.description: Production idempotency must work across concurrent callers and relevant instances.
learningGoals: Concurrent duplicates produce one effect
Crash recovery and retention are specified
examples: Two callers submit refund key K.

tasks.title: Explain Idempotency in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Production idempotency must work across concurrent callers and relevant instances. Define key ownership, payload consistency, retention, and atomic coordination with the effect. A duplicate arriving while work is in progress needs a defined outcome.

workedExample.scenario: Two callers submit refund key K.
steps: One claims K atomically.
The other waits or receives a documented in-progress result.

commonMistakes: Saving the idempotency result after the effect without an atomic plan can leave a crash gap.
material.independentExercise: Implement durable reservation idempotency and inject a crash around result storage.
recallQuestions: What ties the key to the effect?
What happens during in-progress work?

acceptanceCriteria: Concurrent duplicates produce one effect
Crash recovery and retention are specified

topics.title: Timeout
topics.description: A timeout limits how long a caller waits; it does not necessarily cancel remote work.
learningGoals: Total waiting is bounded
Late completion cannot create an unhandled duplicate effect
examples: A remote charge finishes after the caller times out.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A timeout limits how long a caller waits; it does not necessarily cancel remote work. Allocate a total request budget across dependencies and retries. Distinguish a local timeout from a confirmed remote rejection and plan reconciliation when needed.

workedExample.scenario: A remote charge finishes after the caller times out.
steps: The caller cannot assume no charge occurred.
A lookup or idempotent retry resolves the outcome.

commonMistakes: Increasing every timeout can hide a bottleneck while exhausting capacity.
material.independentExercise: Design timeout behavior for a notification dependency without holding database locks.
recallQuestions: What work may continue after timeout?
How is uncertainty resolved?

acceptanceCriteria: Total waiting is bounded
Late completion cannot create an unhandled duplicate effect

topics.title: Concurrency
topics.description: Concurrency includes overlapping work inside one process and across multiple instances.
learningGoals: The invariant holds across instances
Local-only guarantees are labeled explicitly
examples: Two application instances rotate token X.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Concurrency includes overlapping work inside one process and across multiple instances. Identify which authority owns shared state, then choose coordination at that boundary. A Java lock protects only cooperating threads in its process.

workedExample.scenario: Two application instances rotate token X.
steps: Both can acquire their own local lock.
The database must arbitrate the shared claim.

commonMistakes: A process-local lock is not a distributed guarantee.
material.independentExercise: Run the rotation race against shared persistence using two service instances.
recallQuestions: Who coordinates competing writes?
What assumptions change with another instance?

acceptanceCriteria: The invariant holds across instances
Local-only guarantees are labeled explicitly

topics.title: Transaction boundaries
topics.description: Choose a transaction boundary around changes that must commit together.
learningGoals: Atomic changes share a boundary
External effects have a documented recovery plan
examples: Commit a reservation and durable notification intent.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Choose a transaction boundary around changes that must commit together. External network effects need a separate failure strategy because the database cannot undo them. Keep lock duration short while preserving domain atomicity.

workedExample.scenario: Commit a reservation and durable notification intent.
steps: Send the notification afterward.
Track and retry delivery separately.

commonMistakes: Calling a remote service inside a transaction does not make the remote effect transactional.
material.independentExercise: Specify when durable delivery intent is needed and when a simple retry suffices.
recallQuestions: Which effects can roll back together?
When is an outbox justified?

acceptanceCriteria: Atomic changes share a boundary
External effects have a documented recovery plan

topics.title: Failure recovery
topics.description: Recovery starts by asking what durable evidence remains after interruption.
learningGoals: Each crash point has an explicit recovery action
Recovery preserves the business invariant
examples: A reservation commits before notification delivery.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Recovery starts by asking what durable evidence remains after interruption. For each crash point, identify committed state and the next safe action. Add persistent recovery mechanisms only when the feature's delivery or correctness requirements need them.

workedExample.scenario: A reservation commits before notification delivery.
steps: The reservation remains valid.
A durable pending record allows later delivery if guaranteed notification is required.

commonMistakes: An in-memory retry list disappears with the process.
guidedExercise: Mark crash points in a sequence
List durable state at each point
material.independentExercise: Restart a worker after injected failure and verify safe recovery.
recallQuestions: What survives the crash?
Which action is safe to repeat?

acceptanceCriteria: Each crash point has an explicit recovery action
Recovery preserves the business invariant

topics.title: Audit trail
topics.description: An audit trail records meaningful state-changing actions for accountability.
learningGoals: Committed actions have traceable safe records
Retention and integrity requirements are explicit

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: An audit trail records meaningful state-changing actions for accountability. Define who acted, what changed, when, and the outcome with safe identifiers. Operational debug logs and business audit records have different retention and integrity needs.

steps: Record actor, session, timestamp, and result.
Do not retain the raw credential as evidence.

commonMistakes: Logging a message is not automatically a reliable audit trail.
material.independentExercise: Explain how an audit event stays consistent with a committed state change.
recallQuestions: What makes the record useful for accountability?
Which personal or secret data is unnecessary?

acceptanceCriteria: Committed actions have traceable safe records
Retention and integrity requirements are explicit

topics.title: Scalability
topics.description: Scalability asks how the system behaves as traffic or data grows.
learningGoals: Scale decisions follow measurements
State and coordination assumptions are explicit
examples: One instance stores rate limits in memory.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Scalability asks how the system behaves as traffic or data grows. Measure the limiting resource before adding infrastructure. Moving from one instance to several changes assumptions about memory, locks, timers, and job ownership.

workedExample.scenario: One instance stores rate limits in memory.
steps: A second instance doubles independent allowances.
A shared enforcement design is needed if the original global rule must hold.

commonMistakes: Adding replicas can change correctness, not only capacity.
material.independentExercise: Explain which auth state must be shared before running two instances.
recallQuestions: What resource limits throughput?
Which invariant changes with replication?

acceptanceCriteria: Scale decisions follow measurements
State and coordination assumptions are explicit

topics.title: Security
topics.description: Security begins with identifying untrusted inputs, protected assets, and allowed authority.
learningGoals: Threats map to specific controls and tests
Privileges and secret exposure are minimized
examples: A caller supplies another user's session ID.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Security begins with identifying untrusted inputs, protected assets, and allowed authority. Apply least privilege and defense in depth rather than one universal control. Revisit the model after adding a new dependency, deployment boundary, or credential type.

workedExample.scenario: A caller supplies another user's session ID.
steps: Treat the ID as untrusted input.
Authorize ownership using the authenticated principal.

commonMistakes: A framework dependency does not supply your complete threat model.
guidedExercise: Draw trust boundaries and secret flows
Identify one abuse case per boundary
material.independentExercise: Review the auth service for enumeration, replay, cross-user access, and credential leakage.
recallQuestions: Which asset is at risk?
What authority does this component actually need?

acceptanceCriteria: Threats map to specific controls and tests
Privileges and secret exposure are minimized

topics.title: Deployment and configuration

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Deployment should run a reproducible artifact with validated environment-specific configuration.
learningGoals: The artifact runs outside the development IDE
Secrets are supplied safely and invalid settings fail early

material.explanation: Deployment should run a reproducible artifact with validated environment-specific configuration. Keep real secrets out of source and images, and distinguish building from running. A successful local launch does not prove the deployment has correct permissions or dependencies.

steps: Supply database and signing configuration at runtime.
Reject missing required values before serving traffic.

commonMistakes: Copying your local environment file into an image can expose production credentials.
material.independentExercise: Run the service from a clean environment with a local database and migrations.
recallQuestions: What is fixed in the artifact?
Which configuration should fail startup?

acceptanceCriteria: The artifact runs outside the development IDE
Secrets are supplied safely and invalid settings fail early

topics.title: Health checks and graceful shutdown

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Health checks answer specific operational questions.
learningGoals: Health signals have distinct purposes
Shutdown and incomplete work have bounded outcomes
examples: An instance starts before database readiness.

material.explanation: Health checks answer specific operational questions. Liveness concerns whether restart may help; readiness concerns whether an instance should accept traffic. On shutdown, stop accepting work and handle in-flight operations within a bounded policy.

workedExample.scenario: An instance starts before database readiness.
steps: Keep it out of normal traffic until ready.
Do not expose sensitive health details publicly.

commonMistakes: Treating every dependency outage as liveness failure can cause restart loops.
material.independentExercise: Observe an in-flight request during service shutdown and record its outcome.
recallQuestions: When should traffic stop?
When would restart make matters worse?

acceptanceCriteria: Health signals have distinct purposes
Shutdown and incomplete work have bounded outcomes

topics.title: Capacity limits and backpressure

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Bound resources such as connection pools, worker queues, and pending requests.
learningGoals: Pending work remains bounded
Overload produces a deliberate response
examples: A worker queue reaches its limit.

material.explanation: Bound resources such as connection pools, worker queues, and pending requests. Backpressure slows or rejects admission when capacity is exhausted instead of accumulating unbounded work. Decide which response and retry advice clients receive.

workedExample.scenario: A worker queue reaches its limit.
steps: Reject or defer admission under policy.
Keep memory bounded while processing existing jobs.

commonMistakes: An unbounded queue turns overload into delayed failure and memory exhaustion.
guidedExercise: Identify every unbounded collection or queue
Choose a capacity and rejection policy
material.independentExercise: Load a small worker beyond capacity and measure queue size and latency.
recallQuestions: What resource saturates first?
How should a caller react to rejection?

acceptanceCriteria: Pending work remains bounded
Overload produces a deliberate response

topics.title: Operational failure drills

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: A failure drill deliberately injects a known disruption and checks both behavior and recovery.
learningGoals: Injected failures preserve stated invariants
The recovered system completes a new valid operation
examples: Stop the database during an operation.

material.explanation: A failure drill deliberately injects a known disruption and checks both behavior and recovery. State the expected invariant before the drill, capture safe evidence, and verify the system can resume useful work. Do not rely on a happy-path smoke test alone.

workedExample.scenario: Stop the database during an operation.
steps: Observe the safe response and incomplete work.
Restore it and check state plus recovery.

commonMistakes: An error log alone does not prove recovery succeeded.
guidedExercise: Choose duplicate, timeout, and crash drills
material.independentExercise: Run three local drills and write a short incident-style report.
recallQuestions: Which invariant must survive?
What observation proves recovery?

acceptanceCriteria: Injected failures preserve stated invariants
The recovered system completes a new valid operation

exercises.title: Failure Walkthrough
exercises.description: Turn operational questions into local, observable failure drills.
learningGoals: Turn operational questions into local, observable failure drills.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: A rotation transaction fails after its first write.

tasks.title: What if the request happens twice?
What if the database dies halfway?
What if an external API times out?
What if the application crashes?
What if multiple application instances execute this?
What should be logged?
What should never be logged?
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Predicted invariants are compared with observed state
Verify: Duplicate and concurrent actions do not add extra effects
Verify: Timeout uncertainty is handled explicitly
Verify: Recovery is followed by a successful new operation

requirements: What if a request happens twice?
What if the database dies halfway?
What if an external API times out?
What if the application crashes?
What if two instances execute the operation?
Specify safe logging and metrics for each outcome
Identify the durable state and safe recovery action after each interruption
constraints: No production disruption or extra infrastructure required
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: Write predicted outcomes before injecting failures. The report should separate business rejection, partial execution prevented by transactions, and external uncertainty. Recovery is complete only when state is consistent and new valid work succeeds.

workedExample.scenario: A rotation transaction fails after its first write.
steps: The invariant predicts no committed child and an unchanged parent.
The database check verifies that prediction after rollback.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Choose a feature and mark side-effect boundaries.
Inject one failure at each important boundary.
Restore dependencies and submit a new valid request.
material.independentExercise: Run a lost-response scenario and explain why the retry follows the security policy rather than creating a second child.
recallQuestions: What survives each failure?
Which observation proves recovery?

acceptanceCriteria: Predicted invariants are compared with observed state
Duplicate and concurrent actions do not add extra effects
Timeout uncertainty is handled explicitly
Recovery is followed by a successful new operation

exercises.title: Local Deployment Runbook

tasks.title: Verify: The documented clean-start path works
Verify: Invalid required settings fail before accepting traffic
Verify: No real credentials appear in source, artifact, or logs
Verify: Health and shutdown behavior match the runbook

exercises.description: Run the final service outside the IDE with safe configuration and health behavior.
learningGoals: Run the final service outside the IDE with safe configuration and health behavior.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: Start from a clean checkout and an empty local database.
requirements: Build a reproducible service artifact
Run locally with PostgreSQL and migrations
Supply secrets outside tracked source and the artifact
Document required configuration and safe startup failures
Expose controlled health behavior and observe shutdown
Describe how to back up local test data and start from a clean environment
constraints: The roadmap app itself gains no backend
No cloud account, Kubernetes, Redis, or broker needed
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified
Build, run, migrate, diagnose, and stop commands

material.explanation: A runbook turns implicit setup knowledge into a repeatable local operation. Treat configuration errors and graceful stop as testable behaviors. The task is a working small deployment, not a collection of speculative platform components.

workedExample.scenario: Start from a clean checkout and an empty local database.
steps: Build, configure, and migrate before serving requests.
Remove a required setting and verify a clear safe startup failure.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Run the artifact without the IDE.
Observe readiness and an in-flight request during shutdown.
material.independentExercise: Have a fresh shell follow the runbook and record every hidden assumption you discover.
recallQuestions: What secrets are outside the artifact?
What evidence shows the process is ready?

acceptanceCriteria: The documented clean-start path works
Invalid required settings fail before accepting traffic
No real credentials appear in source, artifact, or logs
Health and shutdown behavior match the runbook

challenges.title: Authentication Service
challenges.description: Ship a locally runnable auth service and prove it survives the important failure cases.
learningGoals: Ship a locally runnable auth service and prove it survives the important failure cases.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: U1 registers, logs in, accesses its own API, and rotates X into Y.

tasks.title: Requirements and rules
Data model and migrations
Algorithm and responsibilities
Implementation
Unit and integration tests
Concurrency tests
Failure recovery and observability plan
Verify: A clean checkout builds, migrates, runs, and tests through documented commands
Verify: All required flows work with safe failure responses
Verify: Passwords use a vetted scheme and raw passwords/tokens never persist or enter logs
Verify: Access JWT validation checks the declared algorithm, key, issuer, audience, and time policy
Verify: One parent cannot create two committed replacement tokens
Verify: Replay revocation remains durable after the public rejection
Verify: Cross-user access and revocation are forbidden
Verify: Expiry, duplicate, concurrent, rollback, and lost-response cases have evidence
Verify: Health, configuration, and shutdown behavior match the runbook
Verify: Local drills preserve invariants and demonstrate recovery

requirements: Register and login using a vetted password verifier
Issue short-lived signed access JWTs with explicit validation policy
Issue secure opaque refresh tokens and persist hashes only
Implement rotation, token family, reuse detection, session revocation, logout, and logout-all
Enforce session ownership using the authenticated principal
Implement absolute expiry, abuse limits, and safe generic credential failures
Document access-JWT revocation limitations and lost-refresh-response recovery
Produce migrations, safe diagnostics, health behavior, and a local runbook
constraints: Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Flyway, JUnit, Testcontainers
No Redis, broker, Kubernetes, social login, or full OAuth server initially
Use established security libraries; do not implement signing or password hashing primitives
Run drills locally with disposable data
deliverables: Algorithms, responsibility table, and API contracts
Unit, HTTP, database, and concurrent tests

material.explanation: The final project integrates the existing modules rather than adding a new architecture. Complete one coherent vertical slice at a time: registration, login, protected access, refresh, then revocation and failure recovery. Each slice must demonstrate its stated security and persistence guarantees.

workedExample.scenario: U1 registers, logs in, accesses its own API, and rotates X into Y.
steps: Replaying X triggers the declared family policy.
Logout-all revokes U1 sessions while sessions of another user remain untouched.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Start with a minimal register/login slice and tests.
Add protected ownership checks, rotation, and revocation.
Run duplicate, competing-use, database-failure, lost-response, and shutdown drills.
material.independentExercise: Run the project from a clean checkout, explain every significant class and transaction boundary, and review a foreign-session attack without consulting notes.
recallQuestions: Why does each transaction boundary exist?
What remains uncertain after a timeout or lost response?
